genZNote: Bipolar staining gives it a 'safety pin' look, and it's non-motile — unusual enough among Yersinia to be worth remembering.

morphology.arrangement: Single cells, sometimes bipolar ("safety pin") staining

habitat.hostAssociation: Zoonotic — wild rodents are the main reservoir, transmitted by flea bite
habitat.environmentalOccurrence: Endemic in wild rodent populations in parts of the Americas, Africa, and Asia
habitat.reservoir: Wild rodents (e.g. prairie dogs, rats); flea vector (Xenopsylla cheopis)

microscopy.appearance: Gram-negative coccobacilli with characteristic bipolar ("safety pin") staining

culture.growthCharacteristics: Slow growing at 37°C; grows better at 25-28°C
culture.colonyMorphology: Small, gray, non-hemolytic colonies, described as "fried-egg"/"hammered copper" with prolonged incubation

identificationClues: Bipolar ("safety pin") staining on Wayson/Giemsa stain of lymph node aspirate or blood
Non-motile, unlike most other Yersinia and Enterobacterales
Slow-growing on routine media — requires longer incubation
History of flea exposure or contact with rodents in an endemic area

diseases: Pneumonic plague (person-to-person via respiratory droplets, rapidly fatal if untreated)
virulenceFactors: Type III secretion system (Yop virulence proteins)
clinicalImportance.transmission: Flea bite (bubonic), inhalation of respiratory droplets from a pneumonic-plague patient, or handling infected animal tissue
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: Endemic in wild rodent populations in the western US, parts of Africa, Asia, and South America; historically responsible for pandemics including the Black Death; a recognized potential bioterrorism agent
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: Requires biosafety precautions in the laboratory; bipolar staining is a classic rapid clue while definitive identification/confirmatory testing is pursued

examFacts.importantTest: Wayson/Giemsa stain showing bipolar ("safety pin") morphology
examFacts.distinguishingFeature: Non-motile, unlike most other Yersinia species and Enterobacterales
